evidence.paraphrase: The narrator concludes she herself is an experiment.
evidence.quote: For I feel like an experiment, I feel exactly like an experiment; it would be impossible for a person to feel more like an experiment than I do, and so I am coming to feel convinced that that is what I AM--an experiment; just an experiment, and nothing more.

evidence.paraphrase: She describes the world as recently and imperfectly finished, as if newly constructed.
evidence.quote: In the rush of finishing up yesterday, the mountains were left in a ragged condition, and some of the plains were so cluttered with rubbish and remnants that the aspects were quite distressing.

evidence.paraphrase: She depicts the moon as a physical ornament that fell out of the cosmic scheme.
evidence.quote: The moon got loose last night, and slid down and fell out of the scheme--a very great loss; it breaks my heart to think of it.

evidence.paraphrase: She experiments by trying to physically reach the stars and is surprised they are unreachable.
evidence.quote: When they first showed, last night, I tried to knock some down with a pole, but it didn't reach, which astonished me; then I tried clods till I was all tired out, but I never got one.

evidence.paraphrase: She notes the stars are far off despite appearances, learning about distance.
evidence.quote: You would be surprised to find how far off they are, for they do not look it.

evidence.paraphrase: She reports improving her understanding of distances through trial.
evidence.quote: Today I am getting better ideas about distances.

evidence.paraphrase: She observes the other creature at a distance to determine its purpose.
evidence.quote: I followed the other Experiment around, yesterday afternoon, at a distance, to see what it might be for, if I could.

evidence.paraphrase: She is initially afraid of the man but realizes he is avoiding her.
evidence.quote: I was afraid of it at first, and started to run every time it turned around, for I thought it was going to chase me; but by and by I found it was only trying to get away

evidence.paraphrase: She identifies the novel substance as fire, which she had never encountered before.
evidence.quote: I was curious to know what the pink dust was.  Suddenly the name of it occurred to me, though I had never heard of it before.  It was FIRE!

evidence.paraphrase: She claims to have introduced fire, a new thing, into the world.
evidence.quote: I had created something that didn't exist before; I had added a new thing to the world's uncountable properties

evidence.paraphrase: She names the first flames ever to exist and reacts with rapture.
evidence.quote: Soon brilliant yellow and red flares shot up through the smoke, and I named them in an instant--FLAMES--and I was right, too, though these were the very first flames that had ever been in the world.

evidence.paraphrase: Through fire she discovers the new emotion of fear.
evidence.quote: the fire had revealed to me a new passion --quite new, and distinctly different from love, grief, and those others which I had already discovered--FEAR.  And it is horrible!

evidence.paraphrase: Adam contrasts his and Eve's opposite reactions to the brontosaurus.
evidence.quote: When the mighty brontosaurus came striding into camp, she regarded it as an acquisition, I considered it a calamity; that is a good sample of the lack of harmony that prevails in our views of things.

evidence.paraphrase: She articulates a method of proving things by experiment rather than conjecture.
evidence.quote: It is best to prove things by actual experiment; then you KNOW; whereas if you depend on guessing and supposing and conjecturing, you never get educated.

evidence.paraphrase: She reasons from cumulative evidence to a conclusion she cannot yet prove.
evidence.quote: By experiment I know that wood swims, and dry leaves, and feathers, and plenty of other things; therefore by all that cumulative evidence you know that a rock will swim; but you have to put up with simply knowing it, for there isn't any way to prove it

evidence.paraphrase: She describes repeated experimentation about whether water runs uphill.
evidence.quote: I have experimented and experimented until now I know it never does run uphill, except in the dark.  I know it does in the dark, because the pool never goes dry

evidence.paraphrase: She offers an optical-illusion explanation for observed phenomena.
evidence.quote: Of course it DOESN'T come down, but why should it SEEM to? I suppose it is an optical illusion.

evidence.paraphrase: She reasons from observed shooting stars to the conclusion that all stars may one day vanish.
evidence.quote: By watching, I know that the stars are not going to last. I have seen some of the best ones melt and run down the sky. Since one can melt, they can all melt; since they can all melt, they can all melt the same night.

evidence.paraphrase: She travels widely across the new world and calls herself its first traveler.
evidence.quote: We have made long excursions, and I have seen a great deal of the world; almost all of it, I think; and so I am the first traveler, and the only one.

evidence.paraphrase: After the Fall, the Garden is lost to her.
evidence.quote: When I look back, the Garden is a dream to me.  It was beautiful, surpassingly beautiful, enchantingly beautiful; and now it is lost, and I shall not see it any more.
